In a rechargeable lithium-ion battery, a charger pushes electrons and lithium ions back the other way, reversing the reaction and storing energy again.

questions.title: How satellites stay in orbit
questions.prompt: How do satellites remain in orbit?

expectedConcepts.label: Gravity constantly pulls the satellite toward Earth
Its high sideways speed means it keeps falling around the Earth
Little air resistance at altitude; low orbits slowly decay

questions.modelAnswer: A satellite in orbit is actually falling toward Earth all the time, pulled by gravity, but it is also moving sideways extremely fast, around 7.8 kilometres per second in low Earth orbit. As it falls, the curved surface of the Earth falls away beneath it at the same rate, so it keeps missing the ground and circles the planet instead. Newton illustrated this with a cannon on a mountain firing faster and faster until the ball never lands. Higher orbits need lower speeds; at about 36,000 kilometres, a geostationary satellite takes exactly one day per orbit, staying above the same spot. At low altitudes, thin air still causes drag, so orbits slowly decay unless boosted.

questions.title: Biodiversity and ecosystems
questions.prompt: What is biodiversity, and why do ecosystems benefit from it?

expectedConcepts.label: Variety of life: genes, species and ecosystems
Diverse ecosystems are more productive and resilient to change
Provides services: pollination, clean water, food and medicines

questions.modelAnswer: Biodiversity is the variety of life at every level: the genetic diversity within species, the diversity of species, and the diversity of ecosystems such as forests, wetlands and coral reefs. Ecosystems benefit because different species play different roles, such as pollinators, predators, decomposers and plants that fix nitrogen, and when many species overlap in their roles, the system can absorb shocks: if one species declines because of disease or drought, others fill in. Diverse ecosystems tend to be more productive and resilient. Humans depend on these ecosystem services for pollination of crops, clean water, fertile soil, flood protection, food and medicines, which is why biodiversity loss is a serious risk.

questions.title: The scientific method, evidence and opinion
questions.prompt: How does the scientific method help distinguish evidence from opinion?

expectedConcepts.label: Form a testable hypothesis that could be proven wrong
Test with controlled experiments or careful observation and data
Peer review and replication reduce bias

questions.modelAnswer: An opinion is a belief that may or may not be backed by evidence. The scientific method is a process for testing beliefs against reality. It starts with a question and a hypothesis that makes a specific, testable prediction, one that could turn out to be wrong. Then scientists collect data through controlled experiments or careful observations, comparing for example a group that receives a treatment with a control group that does not, and measuring results objectively. Results are analysed statistically, published for peer review and, crucially, replicated by other researchers. A claim supported by repeated, independent evidence is far more reliable than one person's view, no matter how confident they are.

questions.title: A narrator's point of view
questions.prompt: How does a narrator's point of view shape a reader's understanding?

expectedConcepts.label: First, second and third person points of view
Limited versus omniscient narration controls what the reader knows
Point of view shapes sympathy, suspense and bias

questions.modelAnswer: Point of view decides whose eyes we see the story through and what we are allowed to know. A first-person narrator, using "I", gives intimacy with one character's thoughts, but we only know what they know and believe, so we may share their biases. A third-person limited narrator follows one character closely from outside. A third-person omniscient narrator can enter many characters' minds and comment on events, giving a broad view. These choices shape our sympathy, since we usually side with the character whose inner life we see, and they control suspense and surprise, because information can be withheld. Telling the same story from a different point of view can completely change its meaning.

questions.title: Theme versus plot
questions.prompt: What is the difference between theme and plot?

expectedConcepts.label: Plot is the sequence of events in a story
Theme is the underlying idea or message the story explores
Example showing both in one work

questions.modelAnswer: Plot is what happens: the sequence of events, conflicts and their resolution. Theme is what the story is about at a deeper level: the central idea or question it explores, such as ambition, justice, love, or the cost of revenge. For example, the plot of Shakespeare's Macbeth is a Scottish nobleman who murders the king, takes the throne and is destroyed by guilt and war. Its themes include how unchecked ambition corrupts, and the relationship between fate and free will. A theme is usually not stated directly; readers infer it from the plot, characters and images. Many different plots can share a theme, and one plot can carry several themes.

questions.title: Symbolism in stories
questions.prompt: How can symbolism add meaning beyond a story's literal events?

expectedConcepts.label: A symbol is an object, character or image that stands for a larger idea
Examples of symbols in well-known works
Symbols add depth and invite interpretation

questions.modelAnswer: A symbol is a concrete thing in a story, such as an object, a place, a colour or an action, that also represents an abstract idea. In The Great Gatsby, the green light at the end of Daisy's dock is literally a light, but it also stands for Gatsby's longing and the elusive American Dream. In Lord of the Flies, the conch shell represents order and democracy, and its destruction mirrors the collapse of civilisation among the boys. Symbols let writers express complex ideas without stating them directly, add layers of meaning, and connect different parts of a work through recurring images, rewarding readers who look beyond the literal events.

questions.title: How satire criticises
questions.prompt: How does satire criticize social or political behavior?

expectedConcepts.label: Satire uses humour, irony and exaggeration to criticise
It targets the foolishness or vices of people and institutions
Examples and its purpose of provoking change

questions.modelAnswer: Satire is a form of writing, or performance, that uses humour, irony, exaggeration and ridicule to expose and criticise foolishness, hypocrisy or abuse of power in people, institutions or society. By making something look absurd, it lets audiences see a problem clearly and encourages them to question it. Jonathan Swift's "A Modest Proposal" ironically suggests the poor sell their children as food, to attack heartless attitudes toward Irish poverty. George Orwell's Animal Farm uses a farm to satirise how the Russian Revolution turned into Stalin's dictatorship. Satire works only if the audience recognises the irony, which is why it is sometimes misunderstood and taken literally.

questions.title: Setting and atmosphere
questions.prompt: How do setting and atmosphere influence a story?

expectedConcepts.label: Setting: the time and place of a story
Atmosphere: the mood or feeling created for the reader
Setting shapes characters, conflict and themes

questions.modelAnswer: Setting is where and when a story takes place: a city, a village, a ship, a historical period, or an imagined world. Atmosphere is the mood the writer creates, such as eerie, hopeful, tense or nostalgic, often through descriptions of weather, light, sounds and surroundings. Together they do much more than decorate the background. A setting shapes characters and conflicts: the strict social rules of nineteenth-century England drive the plot of Pride and Prejudice, and the harsh Yorkshire moors mirror the wild passions of Wuthering Heights. A storm or a gloomy house can build suspense, and a change of setting often marks a change in a character's life.

questions.title: Rhythm in free verse
questions.prompt: How can a poem create rhythm without a fixed rhyme scheme?

expectedConcepts.label: Free verse has no fixed metre or rhyme
Rhythm comes from repetition, line breaks and sentence length
Sound devices: alliteration, assonance and parallelism

questions.modelAnswer: Rhyme is only one way to create rhythm. Free verse, poetry without a regular metre or rhyme scheme, builds rhythm in other ways. Repetition of words, phrases or sentence structures, called parallelism, creates a beat, as in Walt Whitman's long, chanting lines. Line breaks control pace: a short line forces a pause or emphasis, while long lines flow quickly. Varying sentence length creates movement, and natural speech stress gives a cadence. Sound devices such as alliteration, repeating initial consonants, and assonance, repeating vowel sounds, link words together musically. The result can feel closer to natural speech while still being carefully patterned.

questions.title: Why translations change a literary work
questions.prompt: Why do translations sometimes change the effect of a literary work?

expectedConcepts.label: Words carry connotations and cultural meanings without equivalents
Sound, rhythm, rhyme and wordplay are hard to keep
Translators must choose between literal accuracy and recreating the effect

questions.modelAnswer: Translation is never a simple swap of words, because languages do not line up exactly. Many words carry connotations, cultural references, levels of politeness or idioms that have no direct equivalent; a Hindi or Tamil word for a specific family relationship or emotion may need a whole phrase in English. Poetry is hardest, because rhyme, rhythm, sound patterns and wordplay depend on the original language's sounds. So translators constantly choose between being literally accurate and recreating the feeling and effect for new readers. That is why two translations of the same work, such as Tagore's poems or Tolstoy's novels, can feel quite different, and readers sometimes compare several.

questions.title: Character development and theme
questions.prompt: How does character development reveal a story's central theme?

expectedConcepts.label: Characters change, or fail to change, through the story
Choices and consequences show what the story values
Example connecting a character arc to a theme

questions.modelAnswer: Themes are often expressed through how characters change. A character arc, the transformation a character undergoes, or fails to undergo, shows the reader what the story believes about people and life. In Dickens's A Christmas Carol, Scrooge changes from a greedy, isolated miser into a generous man after confronting his past, present and future; that change carries the theme that compassion and community matter more than wealth, and that people can redeem themselves. Tragic characters who refuse to change, such as Macbeth, reveal themes through their downfall. Paying attention to the choices characters make and their consequences is one of the best ways to identify a theme.

questions.title: Magical realism versus fantasy
questions.prompt: What is magical realism, and how does it differ from fantasy?

expectedConcepts.label: Magical realism places magical events in an otherwise realistic world
Characters treat the magic as normal, without explanation
Fantasy builds separate worlds with their own rules; examples

questions.modelAnswer: Magical realism is a literary style in which magical or impossible events occur in an otherwise realistic, everyday setting, and the characters and narrator treat them as completely normal, without explanation or surprise. In Gabriel García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude, a character ascends to heaven while hanging laundry, and the family barely reacts. Salman Rushdie's Midnight's Children gives telepathic powers to children born at the moment of India's independence, mixing magic with real history. Fantasy, by contrast, usually builds a separate or clearly magical world with its own rules and creatures, like Middle-earth. Magical realism often uses magic to comment on real politics, history and society.

questions.title: Strong endings in short stories
questions.prompt: How can a short story create a strong ending with limited space?

expectedConcepts.label: Focus on a single conflict or moment from the start
Foreshadowing prepares a twist or epiphany that feels earned
Final image or line resonates and may leave ambiguity

questions.modelAnswer: A short story has no room for subplots, so a strong ending starts with focus: one main character, one central conflict or moment, and every scene pointing toward it. Writers plant small details early, foreshadowing, so that a twist or a moment of realisation, an epiphany, feels surprising yet inevitable, as in O. Henry's "The Gift of the Magi", where both partners sell their treasures to buy gifts for each other. Many stories end with a resonant final image or line rather than explaining everything, and some deliberately stay open or ambiguous, leaving readers to complete the meaning. The ending should answer the story's central question, even if not in the expected way.

questions.title: Oral traditions and culture
questions.prompt: How do oral traditions preserve culture and history?

expectedConcepts.label: Stories, songs, epics and proverbs passed down by speaking
Memory aids: repetition, rhythm and formulas
Preserve identity, values and history; examples and risks

questions.modelAnswer: Before writing was widespread, and in many communities still today, knowledge was preserved by speaking: myths, epics, songs, genealogies, proverbs and folk tales passed from generation to generation. Oral traditions use repetition, rhythm, rhyme and set phrases to make long works memorable; the Mahabharata and Homer's epics were performed orally for centuries before being written down. West African griots preserve family histories and the deeds of kings in song. These traditions carry a community's values, beliefs, history and sense of identity, and teach moral lessons. Because each telling can change, they are living rather than fixed, and they can be lost when languages and communities decline, which is why many are now being recorded.

questions.title: Faithful literary adaptations
questions.prompt: What makes a literary adaptation faithful without copying every detail?

expectedConcepts.label: Faithfulness to spirit, themes and characters rather than every event
Changes are necessary because media differ
Good adaptations translate techniques to the new medium

questions.modelAnswer: An adaptation, such as a film or series based on a novel, cannot copy every detail: a 400-page novel must fit into two hours, and film cannot easily show a narrator's inner thoughts. So faithfulness is better judged by whether the adaptation keeps the spirit of the original: its central themes, the essential nature of the characters, the tone, and the emotional journey. Good adaptations find new ways to achieve the same effect in their medium, using visuals, music or performance where the novel used description, and they may merge characters or cut subplots. An adaptation that copies every event but changes the meaning is less faithful than one that changes events but keeps the heart of the story.

questions.title: Different interpretations backed by evidence
questions.prompt: How can readers interpret a work differently while still using evidence?

expectedConcepts.label: Literary works are open to multiple valid interpretations
Interpretations must be supported by evidence from the text
Different lenses and contexts lead to different readings

questions.modelAnswer: Rich literary works are often ambiguous, and readers bring different experiences and perspectives, so several interpretations can be valid. But not every interpretation is equally strong: a good one is supported by evidence from the text itself, such as specific quotations, repeated images, character choices and structure, and it accounts for details that might contradict it. For example, one reader might see Hamlet's delay as caused by moral doubt, another by depression, and each can cite speeches supporting their view. Different critical lenses, such as historical, feminist or postcolonial, highlight different aspects of the same text. Discussion is valuable precisely because evidence-based disagreements reveal more of the work.

questions.title: The urban heat-island effect
questions.prompt: What is urban heat-island effect, and how can cities reduce it?

expectedConcepts.label: Cities are hotter than surrounding countryside, especially at night
Causes: concrete and asphalt absorb heat, less vegetation, waste heat
Solutions: trees, green roofs, reflective surfaces, water bodies

questions.modelAnswer: An urban heat island is a city that is noticeably warmer than the surrounding countryside, often by several degrees, especially at night. Concrete, asphalt and dark roofs absorb sunlight during the day and release the heat slowly after sunset. Cities have fewer trees and less soil, so there is less cooling from shade and evaporation, and air conditioners, vehicles and industry add waste heat, while tall buildings trap warm air. This increases energy use, air pollution and heat-related illness. Cities can reduce it by planting trees and creating parks, using green roofs and reflective cool roofs and pavements, protecting lakes and wetlands, and designing streets that allow air to flow.

questions.title: Watersheds and water management
questions.prompt: How do watersheds influence water management?

expectedConcepts.label: A watershed is all the land draining into one river or lake
Upstream activities affect water quality and quantity downstream
Management must cover the whole basin across boundaries

questions.modelAnswer: A watershed, or drainage basin, is the area of land where all the rain and snowmelt drains into the same river, lake or sea, separated from neighbouring watersheds by ridges and high ground. Because water flows downhill, what happens anywhere upstream affects everyone downstream: deforestation increases floods and soil erosion, factories and farms can pollute the water, dams change how much water flows and when, and heavy pumping lowers water tables. So effective water management treats the whole watershed as one system rather than following political boundaries, coordinating towns, farmers, industry and sometimes states or countries, and protecting forests and wetlands that regulate flow.

questions.title: Desertification and how to slow it
questions.prompt: What causes desertification, and how can it be slowed?

expectedConcepts.label: Desertification is land degradation in dry regions
Causes: overgrazing, deforestation, poor irrigation and drought
Solutions: reforestation, soil and water conservation, sustainable farming

questions.modelAnswer: Desertification is the degradation of land in dry regions, where once productive soil loses its fertility and vegetation and becomes desert-like. It is not mainly deserts expanding on their own; it is largely caused by human activity combined with climate. Overgrazing by livestock, cutting trees for fuel and farmland, poor irrigation that leaves salt in soils, and intensive farming expose the soil to wind and water erosion, while droughts and climate change make it worse. It can be slowed by planting trees and windbreaks, as in Africa's Great Green Wall initiative, rotating grazing, conserving soil with terracing and cover crops, harvesting rainwater, and supporting communities to use land sustainably.

questions.title: Latitude, altitude, distance from the sea and climate
questions.prompt: How do latitude, altitude, and distance from the sea affect climate?

expectedConcepts.label: Latitude: places near the equator receive more direct sunlight
Altitude: temperature drops as height increases
Distance from the sea: oceans moderate temperatures; inland areas have extremes

questions.modelAnswer: Latitude is the biggest factor: near the equator, the sun's rays strike the Earth almost directly all year, concentrating energy, so it is hot, while near the poles the same sunlight is spread over a larger area at a low angle, so it is cold. Altitude matters because air gets thinner and cooler as you go up, on average about six and a half degrees Celsius per thousand metres, which is why Shimla is cooler than Delhi. Distance from the sea matters because water heats and cools slowly; coastal places like Mumbai have mild, maritime climates with small temperature ranges, while places far inland, like Delhi, have continental climates with hot summers and cold winters.

questions.title: Managing a shared river
questions.prompt: What are the challenges of managing a river shared by multiple states or countries?

expectedConcepts.label: Upstream and downstream users have conflicting interests
Competing uses: irrigation, drinking water, hydropower, ecosystems
Need treaties, data sharing and fair allocation, especially in droughts

questions.modelAnswer: Rivers ignore political borders, so states or countries sharing one often have conflicting interests. Upstream users can build dams and divert water for irrigation or hydropower, reducing flow downstream, while downstream users depend on that water for farming, drinking and fisheries and suffer from upstream pollution. Demand grows with population, and droughts and climate change make shortages worse, turning sharing into disputes, such as the long-running Cauvery water dispute between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, or tensions over the Nile and the Indus. Managing shared rivers needs agreements on how water is allocated, especially in dry years, sharing of data on flows, independent bodies to settle disputes, and cooperation on pollution and flood control.

questions.title: How map projections distort the Earth
questions.prompt: How do map projections distort the Earth's surface?

expectedConcepts.label: A sphere cannot be flattened without distortion
Mercator keeps shapes and directions but enlarges areas near the poles
Other projections preserve area or compromise

questions.modelAnswer: You cannot flatten the surface of a sphere onto paper without stretching or tearing it, just as you cannot flatten an orange peel perfectly. So every map projection distorts something: area, shape, distance or direction. The Mercator projection, designed for sea navigation, preserves angles and local shapes, so a straight line is a constant compass bearing, but it greatly enlarges areas far from the equator; Greenland looks about the size of Africa, though Africa is roughly fourteen times larger. Equal-area projections, such as Gall-Peters, keep sizes correct but distort shapes. Compromise projections, like Robinson or Winkel Tripel, balance the distortions, which is why they are used for world maps.

questions.title: Where major cities develop
questions.prompt: What factors influence where major cities develop?

expectedConcepts.label: Physical factors: water, flat land, fertile soil and natural harbours
Trade routes, crossroads and resources
Political and economic decisions, and growth that attracts more growth

questions.modelAnswer: Historically, cities grew where physical geography made life and trade easier: near rivers and fresh water, on flat, fertile land that could feed people, at natural harbours, and at defensible sites. Locations on trade routes, river crossings and crossroads, such as Kolkata on the Hooghly or Istanbul on the Bosphorus, attracted merchants. Natural resources such as coal, minerals or oil created industrial cities. Political decisions matter too: capitals like New Delhi, Canberra and Brasília were deliberately chosen. Once a city grows, it attracts more people, businesses, infrastructure and talent, an effect called agglomeration, so successful cities tend to keep growing.

questions.title: Sea-level rise and coastal communities
questions.prompt: How does sea-level rise affect coastal communities?

expectedConcepts.label: Caused by melting ice and thermal expansion of warming oceans
Effects: flooding, erosion, saltwater intrusion and storm surges
Responses: sea walls, mangroves, planning and relocation

questions.modelAnswer: Global sea levels are rising because of climate change: water expands as oceans warm, and glaciers and ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica are melting. For coastal communities, this means more frequent flooding at high tides, stronger storm surges during cyclones, erosion of beaches and land, and saltwater seeping into rivers, groundwater and farmland, which damages crops and drinking water. Low-lying places such as the Sundarbans, Bangladesh, Mumbai's coast and small island nations like the Maldives are especially at risk. Responses include sea walls and better drainage, restoring natural defences such as mangroves and wetlands, stricter building rules, early warning systems and, in some cases, planned relocation.

questions.title: Groundwater depletion
questions.prompt: What is groundwater depletion, and why can it be difficult to reverse?

expectedConcepts.label: Pumping water from aquifers faster than it is recharged
Causes: irrigation with free power, urban demand, reduced recharge
Hard to reverse: slow recharge, compaction and land subsidence

questions.modelAnswer: Groundwater is water stored underground in aquifers, layers of rock and sediment. Depletion happens when it is pumped out faster than rain and rivers can recharge it, so water tables fall year after year. India is the world's largest user of groundwater, mostly for irrigation, and in states like Punjab and Haryana, cheap or free electricity for pumps and water-hungry crops like rice have caused steep declines; cities also over-pump while paving over land that once absorbed rain. It is difficult to reverse because some aquifers recharge extremely slowly, over decades or centuries, and when they are over-pumped, the layers can compact permanently, losing storage and causing the land surface to sink.

questions.title: Natural hazards versus disasters
questions.prompt: How do natural hazards differ from disasters?

expectedConcepts.label: A hazard is a natural event that could cause harm
A disaster happens when a hazard meets vulnerable people and places
Preparedness and planning reduce disaster risk

questions.modelAnswer: A natural hazard is a natural event, such as an earthquake, cyclone, flood or drought, that has the potential to cause harm. A disaster happens when a hazard hits people and places that are exposed and vulnerable, causing serious loss of life, property or livelihoods beyond a community's ability to cope. The same cyclone can be a manageable event in one place and a disaster in another, depending on preparation. Odisha shows this well: after a 1999 cyclone killed around ten thousand people, early warnings, cyclone shelters and mass evacuations meant later, similarly strong cyclones killed far fewer. So disaster risk depends on hazard, exposure and vulnerability, and the last two can be reduced.

questions.title: Seasonal water scarcity despite annual rainfall
questions.prompt: Why do some regions experience seasonal water scarcity despite annual rainfall?

expectedConcepts.label: Rain is concentrated in a few months, such as the monsoon
Water runs off quickly when there is not enough storage
Solutions: rainwater harvesting, recharge, reducing losses and demand

questions.modelAnswer: The yearly total of rain can be misleading. In much of India, most rain falls during three or four monsoon months, sometimes in a few intense storms, and the rest of the year is dry. If the water is not captured, it quickly runs off into rivers and the sea, especially from paved cities and degraded land, instead of soaking into the ground. Without enough storage, such as reservoirs, tanks, ponds and healthy aquifers, regions face shortages in the dry months despite heavy rain earlier. Chennai, for example, has seen both floods and severe water crises. Solutions include rainwater harvesting, restoring traditional tanks, check dams that recharge groundwater, and reducing leakage and demand.

questions.title: Public transport, land use and city emissions
questions.prompt: How can public transport and land use influence a city's emissions?

expectedConcepts.label: Transport is a major emissions source, especially private cars
Good public transport reduces car use and emissions per trip
Compact, mixed-use land use shortens trips and supports walking

questions.modelAnswer: Transport is one of the largest sources of greenhouse gases and air pollution in cities, and private cars produce far more emissions per passenger than full buses or metro trains. Good public transport, frequent, reliable and affordable, gives people a real alternative to driving and lowers emissions per trip. Land use matters just as much: spread-out cities with homes far from jobs and shops force long car journeys, while compact, mixed-use neighbourhoods, where housing, offices, schools and shops are close together and built around transit stations, shorten trips and make walking and cycling practical. Combining both, with safe footpaths and cycle lanes, can cut a city's transport emissions substantially.

questions.title: How algorithms shape the news people see
questions.prompt: How do algorithms influence the news people see?

expectedConcepts.label: Feeds rank content by predicted engagement and personal data
This can create filter bubbles and amplify sensational content
Readers can diversify sources and adjust settings

questions.modelAnswer: Most people now get news through social media feeds, search engines and aggregator apps, which do not show everything in time order. Their algorithms rank content by what each user is likely to click, watch, share or comment on, based on past behaviour and data about them. Because emotional, surprising and outrage-provoking content tends to get more engagement, it is often amplified, even when it is misleading. Personalisation can also create filter bubbles, where people mainly see views they already agree with. Readers can reduce these effects by following diverse and reputable sources directly, using chronological feeds where available, and being aware that what they see is curated.

questions.title: Checking a chart before trusting it
questions.prompt: What should a reader check before trusting a chart shared online?

expectedConcepts.label: Source of the data and who made the chart
Axes and scales: truncated axes, inconsistent intervals, units
Context: time range, cherry-picking, per capita or totals

questions.modelAnswer: First check the source: where does the data come from, is it named and reputable, and who made the chart, and do they have an agenda? Then look closely at the axes. A vertical axis that does not start at zero can make small differences look huge; inconsistent intervals or two different axes can create misleading impressions; and units matter. Check the time range, because choosing a specific start and end date can hide or exaggerate a trend. Ask whether it shows totals when per-person figures or percentages would be fairer, and whether it compares like with like. Finally, remember that correlation in a chart does not prove causation.

questions.title: Confirmation bias in public debates
questions.prompt: How can confirmation bias shape political and scientific discussions?

expectedConcepts.label: Confirmation bias: favouring information that supports existing beliefs
Effects: selective sources, polarisation and dismissing evidence
Countermeasures: seeking opposing evidence, peer review, steelmanning

questions.modelAnswer: Confirmation bias is the tendency to search for, notice, interpret and remember information in ways that support what we already believe, while ignoring or dismissing evidence against it. In politics, it leads people to follow sources that agree with them, accept weak claims from their own side and reject strong evidence from the other, deepening polarisation. In science, a researcher may unconsciously design studies or analyse data in ways that confirm a favourite hypothesis. Science counters this with methods such as blind trials, pre-registered studies, peer review and replication. Individually, we can actively seek the strongest version of opposing arguments and ask "what evidence would change my mind?"

questions.title: Opinion pieces versus news reports
questions.prompt: What is the difference between an opinion piece and a reported news story?

expectedConcepts.label: News reports aim to inform with verified facts and sources
Opinion pieces argue a viewpoint and interpret facts
Readers should check labels and separate facts from views

questions.modelAnswer: A reported news story aims to tell readers what happened, based on verified facts, multiple sources, quotes and evidence, and it should present relevant sides fairly without the reporter's personal opinions. An opinion piece, such as an editorial, column or op-ed, openly argues a point of view: it interprets facts, makes judgements and tries to persuade. Both are legitimate, but confusing them is a problem; readers may treat a columnist's argument as established fact. Good publications label opinion clearly. As a reader, check the label and section, notice evaluative language like "disastrous" or "brilliant", and separate the factual claims, which can be checked, from the writer's interpretation.

questions.title: Trade-offs in regulating social media
questions.prompt: What trade-offs arise when governments regulate social media platforms?

expectedConcepts.label: Goals: reduce harmful content, misinformation and protect users
Risks: censorship, restricting free speech and political misuse
Other trade-offs: privacy, encryption and costs for small platforms

questions.modelAnswer: Governments regulate social media to reduce real harms: hate speech, incitement to violence, child exploitation, fraud and coordinated misinformation, and to protect users' privacy and mental health. But every rule involves trade-offs. Requiring fast removal of "harmful" content can lead platforms to over-remove legitimate speech, and vague rules can be used by those in power to silence critics and journalists. Demands to trace who sent messages can weaken end-to-end encryption and privacy. Heavy compliance costs may entrench big platforms while burdening small competitors. Good regulation tends to be precise, focused on processes and transparency, with independent oversight and appeal rights, rather than giving governments broad control over speech.

questions.title: Scientific consensus versus false balance
questions.prompt: How can you distinguish a real scientific consensus from a false balance?

expectedConcepts.label: Consensus: agreement of most experts based on extensive evidence
False balance: presenting both sides as equal when evidence is not
Check major scientific bodies, reviews and expertise

questions.modelAnswer: A scientific consensus is when the large majority of relevant experts agree on a conclusion because many independent studies point the same way, as with human-caused climate change or vaccine safety. False balance happens when media present a debate with "two sides" given equal time, for example one climate scientist and one sceptic, implying that experts are evenly split, when in reality the evidence overwhelmingly supports one side. To tell them apart, look at statements from major scientific academies and organisations, systematic reviews and meta-analyses rather than single studies, and check whether the people speaking have expertise in that specific field. Real scientific uncertainty exists, but it is usually about details, not the core conclusion.

questions.title: Independent journalism in a democracy
questions.prompt: What is the role of independent journalism in a democracy?

expectedConcepts.label: Informs citizens so they can make decisions and vote
Holds powerful people and institutions accountable
Independence from government and owners; threats to it

questions.modelAnswer: Democracy depends on citizens making informed decisions, and independent journalism provides much of the information they need about government, elections, the economy and society. Its most important role is as a watchdog: investigative journalists uncover corruption, abuse of power and wrongdoing by governments, companies and other powerful actors, and those revelations often lead to accountability and reform. Journalism also gives a voice to people and issues that might otherwise be ignored, and provides a space for public debate. To do this, it must be independent of the government, political parties and owners' commercial interests. Threats to press freedom, such as censorship, intimidation or financial pressure, weaken democracy itself.

questions.title: Misleading headlines with accurate articles
questions.prompt: How can a headline mislead even when the article contains accurate facts?

expectedConcepts.label: Headlines exaggerate or oversimplify to attract clicks
They omit context, qualifications or uncertainty
Many people read only the headline, so the wrong impression spreads

questions.modelAnswer: Headlines are short and written to grab attention, so they often exaggerate or simplify. A study finding that a chemical "may slightly increase risk in mice" can become "Common food causes cancer". The article may accurately report the cautious details, the small effect size, the animal study and the scientists' warnings, but the headline drops this context and turns possibility into certainty, or picks the most dramatic quote out of context. Because many people only read headlines and share links without opening them, the misleading impression spreads widely. Readers should read beyond the headline, look for the actual numbers and sources, and be sceptical of headlines that provoke strong emotions.
